You've been at the form guide since breakfast. Every runner, every line, every start. By the end of it you know that race better than anybody in the pub, and you're still no closer to pulling one out of it. Sound familiar? That's not you being slow. That's form study with nothing to hang it on. Ted Davis and Alan Jacobs wrote about exactly that in Practical Punting, back in August nineteen ninety-two. Part two of a piece they called Digging For Winners. They finish it with something you can rule up on a sheet of paper on a Saturday morning. Seven factors, points on and points off. But they don't start there. They start with how much of a horse's form you should believe at all.

One quick thing before we dig in. There's a free companion guide to go with this video, carrying Ted and Alan's full set of factors and every point they hand out. The link's in the description below. Grab it now and you can follow along as we go.

They open with a question. What is Form? Simply put, it's the record of a horse's past performances, and it is your truest and most reliable guide to the horse's ability.

Therefore, they say, we must take great note of Form. And especially take note of recent form, because you'll find that it is the most positive guide you are likely to get when assessing the prospects of any horse in any race. Strong form, in whichever Class the horse happens to be racing, is extremely reliable.

There is, though, a sliding scale of reliability as you take into account the true Class of a horse. That is, the better the horse, the more reliable are the recent form indicators. The more inferior the horse, the more unreliable is the recent form.

Form and fitness are key ingredients of finding winners. Fit horses equal good form. Unless a horse is race-fit, it is most unlikely to produce its best form in a race. The problem facing punters is that they have to work out for themselves, using form as a guide, whether a horse is fit or not.

They believe there are some factors that can be reliably taken into consideration. Firstly, if a horse wins easily when not at the peak of its fitness, you can assume fairly safely that it will improve. In contrast, a horse that wins when at peak fitness is much less likely to show further improvement.

Form changes continually. After each performance, the punter has to decide if a horse is going to improve further, or whether it has peaked and thus entered a downward phase in its campaign. These are the difficulties of form study.

Often, of course, a horse may not need to improve in order to post a win. But, generally, if a horse wins and he is penalised with extra weight, then the horse has to better its previous performance in order to win again.

Now to the date on the form, which they call an essential element of understanding the importance of a given performance. They regard recent form as being between one and fourteen days. Then you get to less recent form, which is a last-start performance between fifteen and twenty-eight days previously. And then doubtful past form, which is a performance of twenty-nine or more days previously. Obviously, the further off a performance, then the more risky is the formline.

Here's how they weight those three, in their own words. If we were to put stars on these three factors, we would award five for recent form, three for less recent form and one for doubtful past form. This gives you a clear indication of the worth of the form as far as recency is concerned. Split into nine sections, say eleven per cent, the recent form is worth fifty-five per cent, as against thirty-three per cent and eleven per cent.

Be wary, then, of form which is dated, or can be termed ancient form. The older it is, the less notice you should take of it. A horse may well have been able to win a twelve hundred metre race twelve months previously, but that win cannot be considered a true pointer a year onwards. You have to search for much more recent form.

The same thing goes for horses resuming from lengthy spells. Their past form can be a guide, but it can be most misleading if the horse returns to racing unfit, and obviously older and possibly slower.

And here they answer the thing you've been muttering at the screen. Bearing all this in mind, they write, we can hear a lot of you remarking that it's all very well to suggest form study, but who has the time or inclination for it? Well, a lot of people do have the time and the inclination, though many of them probably don't do it as thoroughly as they should.

Here's what they propose, then. A method of speedily assessing horses, to be used when you have sorted out the main chances and, hopefully, given each of them a Base Rating. They have devised what they feel is an effective, all-embracing approach to giving penalties and bonuses to the various runners, taking their form into account. You are, in essence, digging deep into the form to find the winners.

The assessments take in the following seven factors. One. Date of last start. Two. Barrier draw. Three. Last-start placing. Four. Improvement. Five. Course ability. Six. Distance ability. And seven. Ability in the going.

New ones go out every day for now, weekly down the track, so subscribe and you'll not have to look. There's more confidence about this game than there is homework. I know which of the two I'd trust. Right you are. Where were we.

Factor one, then. They have already stated that recent form is best form, so the allotment of points for the date of last start factor is along the lines they have already indicated by way of asterisks. That is, five for a last-start run between one and fourteen days previously, three for a last-start run between fifteen and twenty-eight days before, and one point for twenty-nine to forty-two days. There are no points for horses resuming after more than forty-two days.

Factor two. Barriers are not assumed to be of major importance, but obviously in some races at some tracks, you are going to have to take the draw into account in some way. On some tracks, wide draws are difficult to overcome, and they have to be accounted for when you are analysing a horse's chance.

Factor three. Then come the last-start placings, in which they take into account where a horse finished last start. These are important because a great majority of races are won by horses which ran in the first three placings at their last start. And note the condition on that. These points are only given if the horse had its last start within the previous twenty-eight days.

Factor four is the one they expect an argument about. The improvement factor is probably one of the most contentious. They have tried to put it into perspective by deciding on a series of bonuses for the various stages of a horse's campaign, on the assumption that a horse will show the most improvement after the fourth and fifth runs of a preparation. This won't always be the case, but it certainly will be in a large majority of instances.

In the same way they have allotted bonuses for expected improvement, so they have built in a penalty factor for horses which haven't raced for some time. These penalties range from one to ten kilos, or points. The penalties will vary according to how much time a horse has had between its last start and the current start. They will also vary according to the type of horse.

For instance, a twenty-four hundred metre stayer resuming after a long break, and racing over an unsuitable twelve hundred metre trip, will be handed the biggest penalty. Ten. In contrast, a sprinter resuming after a long spell and racing over twelve hundred metres might well be very close to a solid run, and therefore would probably be handed only a two kilo to five kilo penalty on its Base Rating.

In these cases, you will have to use some subjective judgement. In other words, your own opinion. Sometimes you'll be wrong, but many times you'll be right, and that's the name of the game as far as selecting the correct horses is concerned.

Which leaves the last three, and they go together. Then we come to the course, distance and going factors, all very important. A horse which has won on the course is given three points. If it's been placed on the course, it gets one. A horse which has won over the distance gets three points. If it's been placed over the distance, it gets one point. And a horse that's been a winner in the prevailing track going, good, fast, dead, slow or heavy, gets a bonus lift of three points.

Performance on the prevailing track conditions becomes a most important element during the winter months, when tracks are likely to be affected by rain. You must always ask yourself whether a horse can act on the ground conditions. Some horses are hopeless on wet tracks.

They're confident that these factors can be used effectively to pinpoint the major chance in a race, as long as you can just as effectively isolate the top chances to begin with. That is, you examine a field of runners, pick out, say, the top four or five, and then apply their factors.

Better still, if you have access to Class or Weight Ratings. In this regard, they wrote, we cannot do better than point you towards the excellent service provided by George Tafe. If you have Ratings, you can very easily trim a field down to the main chances, simply by looking at the most recent ratings. Then, using their factors, you can put the top fancies through a final grilling to determine which ones earn the most points.

And here's the bit that answers the morning you've been having. If you are a serious punter, you will attempt to bet on only a handful of races. On a Saturday, why not pick out two good races at each meeting in Sydney and Melbourne? That's four races in all. You will have time, then, to study each race carefully.

Draw up their list of important factors on a sheet of paper, write down the name of each of the top four or five fancies in each race, rule off the columns, and then check each horse's form and write in the necessary points.

When you've done this task, you'll have a much clearer idea of which horse has the best chance of winning the race. With just a handful of races to handicap, you'll find it won't take long at all to run through their factors and thus make some real sense of the mysteries of form. Good digging, as they signed it off.

And they left a promise hanging for the next part. The series continues, they wrote, with Ted and Alan showing you how the form factors approach actually operates on real races. These test races will show you exactly how the idea works.

That's the answer to the morning you keep losing to the form guide. Not more form study. Form study pointed at fewer races, with a sheet of paper and seven columns that tell you where to look.

And remember — never bet more than you can afford to lose.
